steelman: Exposing a large MCP tool catalog to a model is not a free convenience; it is a measurable degradation of the model's ability to pick the right tool. Two independent lines of evidence converge. IBM's LongFuncEval measures function-calling accuracy dropping (7.59% to 85.58%, depending on setting) as the tool catalog scales from roughly 8K to 120K tokens on a fixed model, so the loss is an attention/selection effect, not a context-capacity limit. Meta's adaptive-shortlist result shows the fix: retrieving an effective depth of only K=7.4 tools per query reaches 90.3% coverage on BFCL's 370-tool set, statistically indistinguishable from a fixed depth of 50 (90.8%) at one seventh the depth. The engineering conclusion is to treat tool exposure as a retrieval problem: show the fewest tools that still contain the right one. The load-bearing and non-obvious refinement is metrological: raw top-K accuracy or coverage rewards lucky guesses, and in the small-shortlist regime that retrieval creates, the random baseline is large enough (roughly 1/K) to materially inflate the number, so you must chance-correct (Bits-over-Random) before you can read the true selection ceiling or trust any tool-count decision.
strongest_attack: The sharpest attack is not the tired 'long-context models make this moot, just send everything' line (that one loses: LongFuncEval degrades a fixed, long-context-capable model as a function of catalog size, proving the failure is selection under distraction, not window overflow, and cost and latency penalties for a bloated catalog remain regardless). The stronger attack targets the thesis's own claimed novelty, the metric point. Chance-correction is mathematically most impactful when the number of choices is small; at the large catalog sizes where the degradation is dramatic (hundreds to thousands of tools), the random baseline is near zero, so subtracting chance barely moves the number. If the metric adjustment is negligible exactly where the tool-count problem is worst, then 'you cannot see the ceiling until you subtract chance' is trivially true at best and says-nothing-non-obvious at worst, collapsing the thesis into the banal 'retrieval beats dumping everything,' which practitioners already assume.
reconciliation: The thesis survives because the attack's own premise reverses onto it. Chance-correction is negligible for the full 370-tool or 120K-token catalog, true, but the thesis does not recommend evaluating in that regime; it recommends moving to an adaptive shortlist at effective depth K=7.4. At K around 7 the random baseline is roughly 14%, which is precisely large enough to inflate a coverage figure and hide whether a shortlist is winning by skill or by having so few candidates that guessing works. So chance-correction is not a distraction from the tool-count decision; it is load-bearing exactly in the small-depth regime the retrieval fix produces, and it is the tool that lets you compare a depth-7 shortlist against a depth-50 baseline honestly (the 90.3% vs 90.8% comparison is only trustworthy once both are chance-corrected). The metric claim is therefore non-trivial and coupled to the retrieval claim rather than decorative. The two-source convergence also holds: IBM supplies the degradation magnitude, Meta supplies the recovery mechanism and the depth number, and neither is doing the other's job.
strengthened_argument: A large MCP tool catalog is a measurable capability tax on tool selection, demonstrated on fixed long-context models (IBM LongFuncEval: accuracy falls as the catalog grows from 8K to 120K tokens), so the failure is distraction under selection, not window size, and long context does not rescue it. The remedy is to treat tool exposure as retrieval and shortlist to effective depth, which Meta shows recovers essentially full coverage (90.3% at K=7.4 vs 90.8% at fixed depth 50 on BFCL 370 tools) at one seventh the depth. The decision-critical and non-obvious step is metrological and is bound to the retrieval regime, not the full catalog: because retrieval collapses the choice set to a handful of tools, the random baseline becomes large enough to inflate coverage, so you must chance-correct (Bits-over-Random) before trusting any depth or tool-count comparison. Claim precisely: chance-correction matters where you make the decision (small shortlist), which is exactly why it is not trivial.
reason: Each claim is empirically anchored to a distinct source, the two sources are genuinely independent and complementary (degradation magnitude vs recovery mechanism), and the strongest attack, aimed at the thesis's own novelty claim about the metric, is defeated on its own terms: chance-correction is negligible only in the large-catalog regime the thesis abandons and becomes load-bearing in the small-shortlist regime the thesis adopts. The obvious long-context rebuttal also fails because the degradation is measured on capable long-context models and cost/latency penalties persist. The thesis is falsifiable (a shortlist that matched full-catalog coverage with no chance-correction gap would refute the metric point) and non-trivial, so it is defensible.
